common_name: Compact Innocence Nemesia (Fragrant White Trailing Nemesia)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts after hardening off into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Compact Innocence flowers most heavily in cool weather and can pause during peak summer heat.

directions: Plant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, giving light afternoon shade where summers run hot. Compact Innocence is a low, mounding to gently trailing selection of Nemesia caerulea prized for its abundant pure white flowers and a sweet, honey-like fragrance that carries well in containers placed near seating areas or doorways. It flowers most heavily during the cooler months of spring and fall and can slow noticeably once summer heat sets in, so shearing the plant back lightly after a flush of bloom helps it stay tidy and rebound as temperatures moderate. Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged, since nemesia roots are shallow and dislike drying out between waterings.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay above the mid-40s F; KLM is an old, seed-grown heirloom nemesia that performs best in cool spring or fall conditions.

directions: Sow indoors and transplant into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun once cool weather has settled in. KLM is a classic heirloom strain of Nemesia strumosa dating to the mid-20th century, grown for its distinctive two-tone flowers that combine a sky-blue upper lip with a white-and-yellow lower lip, giving each small bloom a tricolor, pansy-like face. Plants form a compact, bushy mound that flowers most freely during mild spring or autumn weather and tends to decline once summer heat and humidity arrive, so treat it as a cool-season bedding plant rather than a summer-long performer. Deadhead spent flower spikes regularly to prolong bloom and keep soil evenly moist through the cool growing season.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts after hardening off into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Ruby Field flowers best in cool weather and can stall during peak summer heat.

directions: Plant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates. Ruby Field is one of the oldest and most enduring diascia cultivars, a South African hybrid discovered in cultivation and named for the gardener who first spotted it, valued for its long trailing stems smothered in small, warm salmon-pink, spurred flowers. It spreads into a loose, low mat that works well spilling over the edge of raised beds, walls, or hanging baskets, blooming most heavily in the cool months of spring and fall while slowing through the hottest part of summer. Shear the plant back by about a third after the first big flush of bloom to keep growth dense and encourage a strong rebloom as temperatures cool.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts after hardening off into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Coral Belle flowers best in cool weather and can decline during peak summer heat.

directions: Plant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing light afternoon shade where summers turn hot and humid. Coral Belle is a long-established diascia hybrid grown for its trailing, well-branched stems covered in warm coral-pink, twin-spurred flowers held just above a low mound of small green leaves. It is an excellent choice for hanging baskets, window boxes, and the edges of raised beds, where the cascading habit can be shown off, and it flowers most freely during mild spring and autumn weather. Cut the plant back lightly once flowering slows in summer heat to tidy the mound and promote a fresh flush of bloom as conditions cool.

planting.note: Plant transplants into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun once frost danger has passed; Whirligig closes its flowers at night and on overcast days, opening fully only in bright sun.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, since flowering slows dramatically in shade or heavy clay. Whirligig is an unmistakable osteospermum cultivar with narrow, spoon-shaped white ray petals that pinch inward before flaring at the tip, radiating like tiny propeller blades around a deep blue-black center disc, giving the whole flower a spidery, pinwheel appearance quite unlike a typical daisy form. Plants form a bushy mound that blooms most heavily in the cooler months of spring and fall and may pause during the most intense summer heat, so a light shearing after the first big flush helps keep growth compact and encourages renewed flowering. Where winters stay mild it can persist as a short-lived perennial, but in colder climates it is best grown as a warm-weather bedding annual.

common_name: Tiger Stripes Gazania (Striped Bicolor Treasure Flower)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost or plant transplants in spring once frost danger has passed; Tiger Stripes opens fully only in sun and closes on cloudy days and at night.

directions: Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained, sandy to loamy soil, since rich or constantly wet soil encourages rot and weak flowering. Tiger Stripes is a striking gazania selection whose bright orange and yellow ray petals each carry a bold, dark radiating stripe down the center, so the flower reads as a pinwheel of contrasting bands rather than a solid color when fully open in sunshine. Plants form a low, spreading rosette of narrow, gray-green leaves and tolerate heat, drought, and coastal salt spray far better than most bedding annuals once established. Deadhead spent flowers regularly to keep the low mound tidy and encourage continuous bloom through the warm season.

common_name: Bossa Nova Orange Begonia (Trailing Bolivian Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants or hanging baskets outdoors after all frost danger has passed; Bossa Nova blooms most heavily with some morning sun but appreciates afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, consistently moist soil in partial shade with a bit of morning sun, ideally in a hanging basket or elevated container where the cascading stems can spill downward. Bossa Nova Orange is a trailing Begonia boliviensis selection grown for its long, arching stems that drape smoothly under a nonstop cover of narrow, flame-orange, angel-wing-shaped flowers from early summer until frost. It tolerates heat and heavy rain far better than large-flowered tuberous begonias, continuing to bloom cleanly without the flowers turning to mush in humid weather, and it is naturally self-cleaning so spent blooms drop away on their own. Pinch the stem tips early in the season to encourage fuller branching, and bring a rooted cutting or tuber indoors before the first fall frost to overwinter it where winters are not reliably frost-free.
